title: Cartridges and calibers: a practical comparison
keywords: Read an ammunition label as separate fields
Compare cost and carried mass without a performance ranking
tldr: Read the complete cartridge or shotshell designation, then compare manufacturer compatibility, sporting context, local availability, package cost and carried mass. Similar names and nominal bullet diameters do not establish interchangeability.
steps: Match the firearm’s chamber marking and manual to the box, including suffixes such as LR, WMR, Luger, NATO and Magnum.
A cartridge identifies the ammunition family. Bullet weight, construction and manufacturer product code identify the particular load within it.
Recoil, weight and ammunition availability are properties of the firearm-and-ammunition combination, not caliber alone.
Hunting rules specify species, seasons, permitted methods and sometimes projectile materials. An emergency does not automatically suspend them.

sections.heading: Caliber, cartridge and bullet: three different things

blocks.caption: Anatomy of a cartridge
blocks.description: Conceptual centerfire cartridge: a bullet sits at the front of a case; the case contains propellant, with a primer at its base. Not to scale; rimfire priming is in the case rim.

blocks.text: Caliber often refers to an approximate bore or bullet diameter. Cartridge is the complete ammunition designation: it describes a particular family with its own case and chamber requirements. Bullet is the projectile, not the entire round. A .22 LR cartridge and a .223 Remington cartridge have roughly similar diameter projectiles, yet belong to very different systems. Shared digits do not establish compatibility.

Rimfire ammunition places priming compound in the case rim; centerfire ammunition uses a primer in the center of the base. Both include a case and propellant. A grain is a unit of mass, not a type of powder: bullet weight printed as “124 gr” is not the propellant charge. Box velocity is a result from a stated test setup and may differ in another firearm.

sections.heading: .22 LR and .22 WMR: inexpensive practice and small game

blocks.caption: Two rimfire families, not interchangeable versions
rows: .22 Long Rifle (.22 LR)
Target practice, introductory sporting instruction and small-game hunting where permitted.
Usually modest recoil, compact ammunition and a broad selection of target and hunting loads.
.22 Winchester Magnum Rimfire (.22 WMR / .22 Magnum)
Small-game and varmint hunting, plus recreational shooting.
A different, larger case; generally more report and higher ammunition cost than .22 LR.

blocks.text: For a household that already owns a lawful sporting firearm, .22 LR can make regular range practice relatively affordable. The cartridge is used in rifles and handguns; the action and specific ammunition still affect reliability and the experience. .22 WMR is a distinct chambering, not a “magnum setting” on a .22 LR firearm. Some revolvers have manufacturer-supplied interchangeable cylinders, but that is a model-specific arrangement rather than permission to mix ammunition.

Small-game hunting is a skill and a regulated activity, not an automatic food plan. Species identification, access to permitted land, seasons, humane harvest and food handling all matter. In Florida, for example, rimfire rifles are not a legal method of taking deer. Lightweight ammunition does not remove those limits or make large-game use appropriate.

sections.heading: Handgun cartridges: names, platforms and real tradeoffs

blocks.caption: Common centerfire handgun cartridges
rows: 9mm Luger / 9×19mm
Semiautomatic pistols and some sporting carbines.
Widely encountered; its common name does not include every cartridge beginning with “9mm.”
.380 Auto / .380 ACP / 9mm Browning Short
Often compact semiautomatic pistols.
Distinct from 9mm Luger. A lighter firearm can feel sharper or be harder to handle than the smaller cartridge suggests.
.38 Special
Commonly revolvers; also some sporting rifles.
A rimmed cartridge. It is not .38 Super or .380 Auto.
.45 Auto / .45 ACP
Semiautomatic pistols and some sporting carbines.
Larger cartridge and typically heavier projectiles than common 9mm loads; not .45 Colt.

blocks.text: A comfortable range firearm depends on grip fit, overall mass, controls and the particular load. A compact pistol is easy to store but may have a less forgiving grip and sight picture than a larger sporting model. It is therefore misleading to promise that a cartridge is “easy for everyone” or rank the whole experience by bullet diameter alone.

Suffixes matter. +P denotes a higher-pressure designation for certain standardized cartridges; it is not an upgrade for any firearm bearing the base name. +P+ is not a single universal SAAMI pressure standard. The firearm manufacturer must authorize the exact ammunition category. Keep ordinary and special-pressure products distinctly labelled rather than combining loose rounds because the headstamps look similar.

sections.heading: .223, 5.56 and the three very different “7.62” names

blocks.caption: Centerfire rifle families
rows: .223 Remington
Target, varmint and other hunting uses where permitted.
Closely related to 5.56×45 NATO, but chamber specifications and ammunition requirements are not identical.
Common in rifles also used for organized recreational shooting.
Do not assume a .223-marked chamber accepts 5.56 ammunition.
.308 Winchester
Target shooting and game hunting with a suitable load and lawful method.
Closely related to 7.62×51 NATO; verify the exact firearm’s authorization.
Some rifles used in sporting and target activities.
The “51” distinguishes this family from 7.62×39.
Sporting rifles used for recreational shooting and permitted hunting.
A different case and chamber from .308 Winchester / 7.62×51.

blocks.text: SAAMI explains that .223 Remington ammunition can generally be used in a manufacturer-confirmed military-specification 5.56 chamber, while 5.56 ammunition should not be assumed safe in a .223 Remington chamber. A .223 Wylde marking refers to a chamber design, not a separate cartridge on the shelf; consult that firearm’s manual. The useful lesson is specific compatibility, not an improvised fit test.

A number such as “7.62” gives too little information to choose ammunition. Case length, shape, chamber standards and intended loading differ. Likewise, “.308 and NATO are the same” is too broad for every firearm, including older examples. Rifle cartridges also tend to add ammunition bulk and report compared with rimfire. Hunting suitability depends on the species, projectile, firearm and law; there is no universal caliber that solves every outdoor task.

sections.heading: 12 and 20 gauge: read the whole shotshell label

blocks.text: Gauge is a historical bore-size system, not a caliber in millimeters. Within this system 12 gauge is a larger bore than 20 gauge; .410 bore is an exception named by bore diameter. A shotgun may use shot, a group of pellets, or a slug, a single projectile. Those are different load types within the shotgun family, not different names for the firearm.

blocks.caption: What a shotshell box tells you
rows: Gauge
The shell family must match the firearm. Do not mix 12 and 20 gauge in one container.
Shell length
The designated length refers to the fired/opened shell, not simply the unfired length in your hand. Match chamber authorization.
Shot size
For common numbered birdshot, a higher number generally means smaller pellets. Buckshot uses another naming scale.
Payload
The quantity of shot, often in ounces; separate from pellet diameter.
Material
Lead, steel and other materials have different properties; hunting and firearm restrictions can apply.

blocks.text: Clay sports and bird hunting often use shotshells selected for the rules of that activity. Bigger gauge, heavier payload or “magnum” branding does not automatically mean better results. Firearm fit, total weight and the particular load affect recoil. Check both firearm and ammunition instructions; a shell slipping into an opening does not prove it belongs there.

sections.heading: Build a comparison that answers your actual question

blocks.text: For a sporting purchase, write down the activity first: affordable paper-target practice, a particular licensed hunting activity or an established club discipline. Compare the cost of routine ammunition, range fees, instruction, secure storage and maintenance as well as the firearm. Availability in your area matters more than an attractive specification from a product you cannot regularly obtain.

items: Record the full chamber designation, exact model and manufacturer-approved ammunition categories.
Compare prices per round within the same cartridge and intended sporting load type.
Keep product codes and lot numbers when you buy; they make recall checks possible.
Reject simple “bigger is better” claims. Cartridge names alone do not describe reliability, accuracy or suitability.
Use the cartridge guide alongside the ammunition-storage guide; identification and condition are separate checks.

blocks.text: For preparedness, preserve the sporting equipment you already understand before adding unfamiliar systems. A labeled, modest inventory that remains secure, dry and identifiable is easier to manage than assorted loose ammunition. Skills, lawful access and realistic expectations give the equipment a purpose; the cartridge label alone does not provide one.

sections.heading: Case shape and primer location are separate descriptions

blocks.text: Rimmed and rimless describe the case-head relationship to the case body. Rimfire and centerfire describe the priming arrangement. The similar words belong to different classifications. A rimmed case can be centerfire; rimless does not mean that the case lacks an extraction surface.

blocks.caption: Case vocabulary in a product description
rows: Rimmed
A projecting rim is wider than the main case body.
Rimless
The head is about the case body's diameter, with an extraction groove ahead of it.
Case mouth
The opening at the forward end of the case.
Neck and shoulder
On a bottleneck case, the narrowed forward portion and the transition to the wider body.
Case length
The case dimension; it is different from the length of the complete loaded cartridge.
Rimfire or centerfire
The priming category, not a guarantee of interchangeability or a case-shape description.

blocks.text: These terms help distinguish specifications that a shortened calibre name conceals. Two products can share an approximate projectile diameter while having different case geometry and chamber requirements. A photograph can show the broad shape but cannot establish the relevant dimensions, pressure standard or manufacturer approval.

Headstamp wording is another identification clue, while the original package identifies the particular product and lot. Neither a similar-looking case nor a round that seems to fit establishes permission to use it. The exact chamber marking, recognized cartridge designation and firearm manufacturer's guidance remain the compatibility evidence. This vocabulary is for reading factory products, not altering or making ammunition.

sections.heading: Mass, speed and package count must keep their units

blocks.text: A grain is a unit of mass used on ammunition labels: 7,000 grains equal one pound. It is distinct from a gram and from a single granule of propellant. A printed projectile mass does not give the mass of a complete cartridge, and it is not a loading instruction.

blocks.caption: Read each figure as its own quantity
rows: Projectile mass in gr
The mass of the projectile specified for that product.
Complete-cartridge or complete-box transport mass.
Payload mass in oz
The specified shotshell payload.
A shell's total mass or chamber compatibility.
Velocity in ft/s or m/s
A speed under the stated test conditions.
An identical result in every firearm or environment.
Package count
The number of factory rounds or shells in the package.
The mass of the packaging or condition of the contents.
Product and lot code
The manufacturer's particular offering and production identity.
Interchangeability merely because another product shares a calibre abbreviation.

blocks.text: An invented unit-reading example illustrates the distinction: a projectile marked 124 gr has a mass of approximately 8.04 g. Fifty such projectiles total about 402 g, but fifty complete factory cartridges also contain cases, primers and propellant, and a transport box adds packaging. Weigh the actual complete package when gross mass matters. Do not substitute projectile arithmetic for a carrier's weight check.

Comparing two velocity listings also requires consistent units and matching test context. Keep the manufacturer's test information with the value rather than treating the largest printed number as a complete account of a sporting product. Availability, compatible factory designation, venue or species restrictions, and ordinary ownership costs are separate questions that a single number cannot settle.

without_help: Set unidentified or mixed ammunition aside in secured, clearly marked packaging. Do not try it in a firearm to discover whether it fits. A photograph of markings and the original box can help the manufacturer identify the product.
household: Use full names on storage labels, including gauge and shell length where relevant. Anyone authorized to manage the inventory should understand that similar numbers and similar appearance do not establish compatibility.
pack_now: Manufacturer, full cartridge name, product code, lot number, quantity, purchase date and the exact firearm manual.
next: List the chambering of each sporting firearm you own and link the corresponding manufacturer manual. Use that list for purchases rather than memory.
watch: Ammunition remains hazardous regardless of its size. Keep it secured and correctly identified; never force a cartridge into a firearm or use damaged, recalled or disaster-exposed ammunition without the manufacturer’s clearance.
